source_user: A speculative decoder is slower than the target model alone. Identify what to measure. Scenario variant 7: include an explicit falsifiable hypothesis and a controlled experiment.
source_assistant: Answer should state assumptions, a falsifiable hypothesis, measurements, expected confounders, and rollback criteria. Minimum technical points: measure draft latency, target verification latency, acceptance rate by position, accepted tokens per step, synchronization overhead, and workload dependence.
corrected_answer:
Assumptions: draft and target use compatible tokenization and an explicitly defined exact or probabilistic verification rule; measurements are on the same hardware, software build, model precision, and serving configuration; and target-only is the comparison baseline. “Slower” must be separated into TTFT, per-output-token latency, end-to-end latency, throughput, cost, and tail behavior. No platform-specific cause is assumed without trace evidence.

Hypothesis: speculative decoding improves performance only when the target work avoided by accepting multiple draft tokens exceeds draft computation plus verification, transfer, synchronization, scheduling, and any queueing overhead. In a matched experiment, speculation will reduce median and p95 TPOT and increase output tokens/s without changing exact output semantics; if acceptance is low or coordination overhead dominates, target-only will be faster. Predeclare a practical threshold, such as a confidence interval for the change in TPOT and a non-inferiority bound for correctness, rather than treating one run as evidence.

Measure with synchronized monotonic timestamps per request and speculation step: TTFT, TPOT, end-to-end latency, p50/p95/p99, throughput, queue time, draft time per token and per step, target verification time and verified batch length, acceptance rate by draft position and workload stratum, accepted tokens per step, rejected-token recomputation, target forward calls, and effective target tokens generated per call. Also record barrier/synchronization and CPU scheduling time, host-device and inter-device transfer bytes/time, kernel launch gaps, GPU utilization, memory/KV-cache pressure, batch size, concurrency, arrival rate, prompt/output lengths, temperature/sampling settings, and energy or cost per generated token. Use traces to avoid incorrectly summing overlapping intervals. Check token counts, termination behavior, logits/seed/configuration, and exact or declared-equivalent outputs against target-only.

Run a randomized, repeated paired comparison of target-only and speculative modes over representative prompt lengths, output lengths, concurrency, arrival-rate, and content strata, with warm-up, fixed seeds where applicable, identical admission and batching policies, and run-order interleaving. Vary draft model/version, draft length, verification batch size, and acceptance rule one factor at a time or via a predeclared factorial design. Report medians and tail quantiles with confidence intervals, plus acceptance and cost decomposition; include a no-speculation baseline and, if possible, a synchronization/transfer microbenchmark. Control for thermal throttling, cache warmness, background load, scheduler placement, clock settings, compilation/autotuning, network contention, memory pressure, batching policy, and measurement overhead.

Rollback or disable speculation if correctness/token accounting diverges, quality falls beyond the predeclared non-inferiority bound, OOM/error/retry rates rise, or latency/cost SLOs regress at agreed quantiles for a sustained canary window. Start in shadow or bounded-canary mode, cap draft length and concurrency, retain target-only fallback, alert on acceptance and tail regressions, and preserve redacted request-level traces. Evidence required: synchronized component traces, matched baseline/speculative trials across workload strata, repeated-run uncertainty, and correctness plus resource/SLO results.

workload, batching, thermal, scheduler, or compilation effects can confound comparisons
verification or sampling changes can alter output semantics
memory pressure and retries can hide the causal component
evidence_required: repeated randomized paired target-only versus speculative trials across workload strata

source_user: A speculative decoder is slower than the target model alone. Identify what to measure. Scenario variant 95: include an explicit falsifiable hypothesis and a controlled experiment.
source_assistant: Answer should state assumptions, a falsifiable hypothesis, measurements, expected confounders, and rollback criteria. Minimum technical points: measure draft latency, target verification latency, acceptance rate by position, accepted tokens per step, synchronization overhead, and workload dependence.
corrected_answer:
Assumptions: draft and target use compatible tokenization and an explicitly defined exact or probabilistic verification rule; measurements are on the same hardware, software build, model precision, and serving configuration; and target-only is the comparison baseline. “Slower” must be separated into TTFT, per-output-token latency, end-to-end latency, throughput, cost, and tail behavior. No platform-specific cause is assumed without trace evidence.

Hypothesis: speculative decoding improves performance only when the target work avoided by accepting multiple draft tokens exceeds draft computation plus verification, transfer, synchronization, scheduling, and any queueing overhead. In a matched experiment, speculation will reduce median and p95 TPOT and increase output tokens/s without changing exact output semantics; if acceptance is low or coordination overhead dominates, target-only will be faster. Predeclare a practical threshold, such as a confidence interval for the change in TPOT and a non-inferiority bound for correctness, rather than treating one run as evidence.

Measure with synchronized monotonic timestamps per request and speculation step: TTFT, TPOT, end-to-end latency, p50/p95/p99, throughput, queue time, draft time per token and per step, target verification time and verified batch length, acceptance rate by draft position and workload stratum, accepted tokens per step, rejected-token recomputation, target forward calls, and effective target tokens generated per call. Also record barrier/synchronization and CPU scheduling time, host-device and inter-device transfer bytes/time, kernel launch gaps, GPU utilization, memory/KV-cache pressure, batch size, concurrency, arrival rate, prompt/output lengths, temperature/sampling settings, and energy or cost per generated token. Use traces to avoid incorrectly summing overlapping intervals. Check token counts, termination behavior, logits/seed/configuration, and exact or declared-equivalent outputs against target-only.

Run a randomized, repeated paired comparison of target-only and speculative modes over representative prompt lengths, output lengths, concurrency, arrival-rate, and content strata, with warm-up, fixed seeds where applicable, identical admission and batching policies, and run-order interleaving. Vary draft model/version, draft length, verification batch size, and acceptance rule one factor at a time or via a predeclared factorial design. Report medians and tail quantiles with confidence intervals, plus acceptance and cost decomposition; include a no-speculation baseline and, if possible, a synchronization/transfer microbenchmark. Control for thermal throttling, cache warmness, background load, scheduler placement, clock settings, compilation/autotuning, network contention, memory pressure, batching policy, and measurement overhead.

Rollback or disable speculation if correctness/token accounting diverges, quality falls beyond the predeclared non-inferiority bound, OOM/error/retry rates rise, or latency/cost SLOs regress at agreed quantiles for a sustained canary window. Start in shadow or bounded-canary mode, cap draft length and concurrency, retain target-only fallback, alert on acceptance and tail regressions, and preserve redacted request-level traces. Evidence required: synchronized component traces, matched baseline/speculative trials across workload strata, repeated-run uncertainty, and correctness plus resource/SLO results.

quality_dimensions.coverage: covers assumptions, mechanism, falsifiable hypothesis, measurements, controlled experiment, confounders, correctness, safety and rollback

quality_dimensions.actionability: provides baselines, randomized strata, instrumentation, canary and fallback
